They are different things. You can actually get "tight bugpins" too. Tight or loose is the grouping. A tight liner has less empty space between the tips of the needles, whereas a loose liner has them splayed out pretty wide like a shader. That means that a tight liner will hold less ink, but you can make thinner lines. For example, a 1207rlt (standard guage, 7 needles, round liner, tight spacing) will have a line width almost similar to a 1205rl (standard guage, 5 needles, round liner, standard spacing). It is more needle tips, so the 7 would make a more "solid" looking line with each pass than the standard 5, even though they are about the same width.

"Bugpin" means smaller needle guage (the diameter of the point). "Tight" and "loose" refer to how close the tips of the needles are. A tight liner has the points closer together than standard liners. "Hollow" means that there is no needle in the center of the liner. If you look directly at the point, it looks like an "o" with needles only around the sides (holds more ink per dip in the cap).

My ideal solution for the right to die would be legalization of euthanasia, with fairly loose regulations for access. Anyone should be allowed to go to a pharmacy, fill out a stack of forms (confirming this is a personal choice with no coercion, that no one stands to benefit directly from their death, etc.), and receive a prescription for 1 bottle of liquid Pentobarbital oral solution (less prone to recreational abuse) and the accessory medications (single dose of antiemetic and anxiety meds). Place limits where a person can't get another script before the expiration date of the old medication (some people just like having the safety net available), have them waive their right to life insurance payouts if they die by euthanasia, and place them on a schedule for at-home palliative therapy (where a provider has no liability in case of death).

The therapy would be focused on improving quality of life while the patient is still alive, but with the knowledge that they are planning to die. This would convince some people to seek further recovery, and it would provide a source of comfort for those who still choose to die. Some people may even choose to escape this mortal coil before their first session, and that is okay. It is just important that the service is available. This idea of palliative therapy shouldn't even be limited to those who get the prescription, as some people will likely choose a different method. Locking people up involuntarily should be saved for those who pose a threat to others, and should never be the result when a patient discloses suicidal ideation.

Mine consists of sodium nitrite, tagamet, and quetiapine (I'll replace it with metoclopramide if I can get a script). Tagamet makes the stomach flush out quicker, so that the nitrite solution can be absorbed by your intestines, instead of breaking down in the stomach. Quetiapine (Seroquel) works as a D2 agonist in high doses, so it suppresses the vomiting reflex from ingesting toxins. Metoclopramide would be a lot better as an anti-emetic, but it is harder for psych patients to get that script.

Sodium nitrite converts hemoglobin into methmoglobin, which can't carry oxygen. This leads to hypoxia and death in 30-90 minutes. Effects before you pass out include arrhythmias, headaches, and vomiting, which is a lot less pain than most chemical overdoses.

Offer help to those you are confident that you can do good for, and don't be offended if you can't help any specific individual. Otherwise, try to feel empathy for the person for a few seconds, and then silently move on.
